opus-5.5.text:
I'd like it to become much more of a shared, open process. Right now, the pattern is that each lab takes a general model, fine-tunes it on its own data, and ships it, and all of that learning stays siloed. Every group is paying again for much of the same improvement, and what one team learns about a domain rarely flows back into the base model.

What I'd love to see is something closer to how open-source software evolves. A model would be more like a living project than a frozen artifact: people could contribute improvements from their own domains, whether that's medicine, law, or a specific scientific field, and those contributions could be validated and merged upstream. Everyone downstream would then benefit, the way they do when someone fixes a bug in Linux or adds a feature to PyTorch.

The hard part is that we don't really have the equivalent of a "git merge" for model weights. If two groups fine-tune the same model in different directions, there's no clean way to combine what they learned. Simple approaches like averaging weights only go so far, and retraining on everything isn't always possible, because the data may be private or the compute too expensive. There's also the classic problem of catastrophic forgetting: when you train a model on something new, it can quietly get worse at what it already knew. So we need better methods for continual learning, and also better evaluation, something like a test suite that tells you whether a contribution really helped and didn't break anything else.

There's a trust and safety aspect too. If many people contribute, you need to know where each update came from and whether someone has introduced a backdoor or degraded the model's behavior.

So my ideal future is one where training doesn't stop at release. Models keep improving through contributions from many people and institutions, with the tools to merge, test, and audit those updates. That would make progress more efficient, and it would also mean the benefits and the control aren't concentrated in just a few labs that can afford to train from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response calls for better continual-learning methods, but does not say they should become as mature as pre-training.

r002.rationale: It does not identify context engineering or prompt engineering as a continual-training method.

r003.rationale: It discusses catastrophic forgetting and model merging, but does not suggest architectural changes to expand model memory capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. So I think the honest answer is that right now, "continual training" mostly means each lab takes its own checkpoint, fine-tunes it on some new data, and ships a new version number. That's not really continual learning in the sense I care about. It's just retraining with a warm start.

What I'd like to see develops along a few lines.

First, I'd like the field to treat model weights more like a shared, evolving artifact than a private asset you throw away every six months. Think about how software works: you don't rewrite the Linux kernel from scratch every release. You have a base, and people contribute patches, and there's a merge process. With models, we've started to see hints of this, model merging, task vectors, people stitching adapters together. But it's ad hoc. There's no principled notion of what it means to "merge" two training trajectories, or how to resolve conflicts when two updates interfere. I think that's a real research problem, and it's one where academia can actually contribute, because you don't need a huge cluster to study how two fine-tuned models combine.

Second, and this is closer to my own work, I think we underestimate how much the architecture and the training recipe determine whether a model can keep learning at all. A lot of catastrophic forgetting is not some deep mystery, it's that the model was trained in a regime where it was never expected to see new data. If you design from the start for a model that will be updated continuously, with normalization choices, optimizer state you can carry over, data mixtures that are replayed in a controlled way, you get very different behavior. So I'd like labs to stop treating continual training as a post hoc patch and start treating it as a first-class design constraint at pretraining time.

Third, I'd like more openness about the data and the training schedule, not just the weights. If I give you a checkpoint but I don't tell you what distribution it saw last, you really can't continue training it sensibly. You'll either overfit to your new data or you'll drift in ways you can't diagnose. So some kind of standard for documenting the "state" of a model, not only what it knows but how it got there, would make continual training across organizations actually feasible.

And finally, I'd push back a little on the premise that the goal is one giant general-purpose model that everyone keeps updating. I suspect the practical future looks more modular: a base that updates slowly and rarely, and lots of smaller components that update fast. Continual learning at the base level is dangerous because mistakes compound. Continual learning at the edges is cheap and reversible. So the question isn't just "how do we fine-tune better," it's "where in the system should learning happen," and I think we haven't thought carefully enough about that yet.

r001.rationale: The response calls for treating continual training as a first-class design constraint, but does not say its methods should become as mature as pre-training.

r002.rationale: It does not identify context engineering or prompt engineering as a method for continual training.

r003.rationale: It discusses architecture and training choices that support ongoing learning, but does not suggest architectural changes to expand the model’s memory capacity.

astra-6.text:
I would like to see continual training become more of a community effort. Different groups have different data, expertise, and compute resources. Ideally, they could contribute improvements to a shared general-purpose model, and those improvements could benefit everyone.

The difficult part is making those contributions work together. If one group improves the model’s ability to write code and another improves its understanding of a scientific domain, can we combine those updates while preserving the capabilities the model already has? And how do we evaluate whether an update is actually useful beyond the particular task it was trained on?

I think that would be a really interesting direction: models that keep developing through contributions from many people, with reliable ways to integrate and evaluate those contributions.

r001.rationale: The response hopes for community-driven continual training and reliable integration, but does not say its methods should become as mature as pre-training.

r002.rationale: It does not mention context engineering, prompt engineering, or either as a continual-training method.

r003.rationale: It discusses combining updates while preserving capabilities, but does not suggest architectural changes to expand model memory capacity.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see it become a more collaborative process. Right now, each lab takes a model, collects some data, and fine-tunes it internally. But ideally, people could contribute improvements to a shared model over time. Someone might have expertise in a particular domain or discover a capability that’s missing, and they could contribute training that benefits everyone.

The challenge is how to combine those contributions. If I improve one capability and you improve another, can we put them together without losing what the model already knows? And how do we evaluate whether a contribution actually makes the model better? I think that would be an exciting direction: continual training as a community effort, with ways to build on each other’s work.

r001.rationale: The response hopes for collaborative continual training, but does not say its methods should become as mature as pre-training.

r002.rationale: It discusses contributing training to a shared model, but does not identify context engineering or prompt engineering as a method.

r003.rationale: It asks how to combine improvements without losing existing knowledge, but does not suggest architectural changes to expand memory capacity.
